findings.category: A01: Broken Access Control / Open Redirect (typosquatting via flawed same-site check)
findings.title: `netloc.lstrip("www.")` does NOT strip the literal prefix "www." — it strips ANY leading characters in the set {w, .}. Attacker-controlled hostnames like `worangetrackdiecast.com` collapse to `orangetrackdiecast.com` and pass the same-site check.
findings.description: Decision 4 specifies: `urlparse(href).netloc.lstrip("www.") == urlparse(source_url).netloc.lstrip("www.")`. Python's `str.lstrip(chars)` treats `chars` as a SET of characters to strip from the left, not a literal prefix. So: - `'www.orangetrackdiecast.com'.lstrip('www.')` → `'orangetrackdiecast.com'` (intended) - `'worangetrackdiecast.com'.lstrip('www.')` → `'orangetrackdiecast.com'` (FALSE POSITIVE — the leading `w` is in the strip set) - `'wwwworangetrackdiecast.com'.lstrip('www.')` → `'orangetrackdiecast.com'` - `'.www.evil.com'.lstrip('www.')` → `'evil.com'` (also strips leading dot — but more concerning: `'.orangetrackdiecast.com'.lstrip('www.')` = `'orangetrackdiecast.com'`) Attack vector: orangetrackdiecast.com is WordPress; their articles often contain editorial outbound links from authors. A malicious or compromised author (or any HTML-injection vulnerability on the source site, comment-area XSS, etc.) embeds `Mercedes`. The parser passes it through `_safe_href` (it's a valid http URL → kept). The bot's same-site check `lstrip("www.")` accepts it as same-site. The Telegraph article published to `@myhwchannel123` then renders it as a clickable link to the typosquatted phishing domain. The bot effectively launders attacker-controlled links into a trusted publisher footprint. This is a typosquatting/open-redirect-assist vulnerability with a CVSS-equivalent of high-impact: it weaponizes the bot as a phishing distribution channel.
findings.location: Section: Decisions § Decision 4 (line 93); Architecture § preview_nodes loop (line 56-59); Task 4 implementation
findings.impact: Bot publishes phishing/typosquatting hostnames to the Telegram channel as trusted-looking inline links. Subscribers click expecting orangetrackdiecast.com content and reach attacker-controlled domains. Reputational damage (Telegram channel implicitly endorses the link). Potential credential phishing if attacker mimics orangetrack login.
findings.recommendation:
Replace `lstrip("www.")` with explicit prefix matching:

```python
def _strip_www(netloc: str) -> str:
    netloc = (netloc or "").lower()
    if netloc.startswith("www."):
        return netloc[4:]
    return netloc
```

Add a regression test:

```python
def test_lookalike_domain_not_treated_as_same_site():
    # worangetrackdiecast.com must NOT match orangetrackdiecast.com
    assert not _is_same_site(
        "https://worangetrackdiecast.com/x",
        "orangetrackdiecast.com",
    )
    # Also: leading dot, repeated `w`, etc.
    assert not _is_same_site("https://wwworangetrackdiecast.com/x", "orangetrackdiecast.com")
```

Additionally, normalize netlocs case-insensitively (urlparse preserves case in netloc) and consider port stripping. Update Decision 4 in tech-spec to specify literal prefix removal, not `lstrip`.
findings.cwe: CWE-1023 (Incomplete Comparison with Missing Factors); CWE-601 (URL Redirection to Untrusted Site)

findings.category: A03: Injection (output rendering — link spoofing via display-text mismatch)
findings.title: `run.text` substring search wraps arbitrary text in `<a>`, allowing display-text/href divergence to mislead readers about link destination.
findings.description: The helper finds `run.text` inside the (possibly LLM-translated) `block.text` and wraps that span as ``. Two concerns: 1. **No constraint that `run.text` resembles a URL or label.** If the source article has `Mercedes-Benz`, the published Telegraph article will show "Mercedes-Benz" as a clickable link to `/very-shady-page`. This is by design for legitimate cross-linking, but combined with the same-site bug above (worangetrackdiecast.com false-positive), the visible text "Mercedes-Benz" can hide a typosquatted href. Subscribers' only signal that the link is suspicious is hovering and reading the URL — but mobile Telegram clients don't expose URL on tap. 2. **First-occurrence wrap means LLM translation drift can move the link.** If the LLM translates `"The Mercedes is fast. The Ferrari follows. Buy a Mercedes here."` to RU and the original run was for the third "Mercedes" (the editorial CTA), substring search wraps the FIRST "Mercedes" — silently moving the clickable affordance to a different sentence. This is acceptable for benign content but combines with finding #1: an attacker who controls source-side anchor text can ensure their link wraps the most prominent occurrence in any translation.
findings.impact: Display-text/destination mismatch is the primary mechanism of phishing. Combined with finding #1 (same-site spoof), an attacker who can plant a single anchor in an orangetrack article (compromised author, comment-section HTML injection if any, site SSO compromise) gets an arbitrary-text → arbitrary-URL clickable link in the published Telegraph article. Even WITHOUT finding #1, an attacker who plants `Mercedes` benefits from the bot republishing it.
findings.recommendation:
Defense-in-depth measures:

1. **Render the href visibly when display text doesn't equal URL host.** If `run.text != run.href` host, append `(<host>)` after the link or footnote-style. Trade-off: visual noise. Alternative: render only if display-text length >= some heuristic match to URL slug.

2. **Skip runs whose `run.text` overlaps multiple sentences** (heuristic for translation drift): if the substring match crosses a sentence boundary in `block.text`, drop to plain text.

3. **Add a length sanity check:** if `len(run.text) > 64` or contains newlines/control chars (unlikely after `_safe_for_ping`-style normalization, but `_runs_from_tag` only `re.sub`s whitespace), drop.

4. **Prefer to render the bare URL if the run.text is short/ambiguous** (e.g., `"here"`, `"link"`, single-word that doesn't match URL slug).

5. Consider an allowlist of href patterns: only links pointing to `/blog/`, `/article/`, etc. paths (not `/redirect`, `/out`, or query strings with `?url=`).

findings.category: A04: Insecure Design (mailto: hrefs leak through same-site check; missing scheme allowlist on the rendering side)
findings.title: `_render_paragraph_with_runs` re-trusts `run.href` without re-validating scheme; combined with mailto: legitimacy in `_safe_href`, an empty-netloc edge case may cause unexpected matches.
findings.description:
`_safe_href` allows `http`, `https`, AND `mailto`. A `mailto:abuse@evil.com` href has `urlparse().netloc` == `''`. After `lstrip("www.")`, it remains `''`. If `source_url` is `None` or somehow has empty netloc (e.g., relative URL passed as source_url, or urlparse failure path), both sides could be empty strings → equal → matched as same-site. Result: a `mailto:` run gets rendered as an `<a>` node in Telegraph, opening a mail client to the attacker's address.

Additionally, the spec doesn't say `_render_paragraph_with_runs` re-validates `run.href` scheme. Defense in depth (don't trust upstream filter): if `_runs_from_tag` ever changes its `_safe_href` allowlist, the renderer silently inherits the new permissiveness.
findings.location: Section: Decisions § Decision 4 (line 93-97); _render_paragraph_with_runs design; _safe_href at orangetrack_source.py:198
findings.impact: Phishing/spam vector: published article contains `click for VIN check` where the visible text and mailto: target diverge. Some Telegram in-app browsers or Instant View renderers may auto-trigger mail compose. Also, scheme drift from upstream filter creates a hidden coupling.
findings.recommendation:
1. In `_is_same_site` (or `_render_paragraph_with_runs`), explicitly require BOTH parsed netlocs to be non-empty before comparing. Reject when either is empty.

2. Add an explicit scheme check inside the renderer: only render `<a>` for `http`/`https` schemes. Drop `mailto`/`tel`/etc. (or make the allowlist explicit). This makes the renderer's contract independent of the parser.

3. Add a unit test:

```python
def test_mailto_run_dropped():
    runs = [{"text": "contact", "href": "mailto:x@y.com"}]
    nodes = _render_paragraph_with_runs("Please contact us", runs, "https://orangetrackdiecast.com/article")
    assert all("a" != n.get("tag") for n in nodes if isinstance(n, dict))
```

4. Add a unit test for empty source_url netloc (e.g., `source_url=None`, `source_url=""`, `source_url="/relative"`) — asserts NO link rendered.
findings.cwe: CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation); CWE-345 (Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity)

findings.category: A04: Insecure Design (DoS — quadratic substring search on adversarially long input)
findings.title: `_render_paragraph_with_runs` does N substring searches over `block.text`; both N and `len(text)` are RSS-controlled. Worst case is O(N × M) with no documented cap.
findings.description:
Tech-spec says "iterates runs in their original order, ... finds the first occurrence of run.text in text (case-sensitive str.find), records the (start, end, href) span". If a malicious source article emits a paragraph with 1,000 anchors and a 1 MB text body (orangetrack content cap is 5 MB per `MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE`), this becomes ~10^9 operations. `str.find` is C-fast but still linear; combined with the per-block invocation in `preview_nodes` and per-article invocation in the cron job, a single crafted source page could pin the bot for several seconds.

The `MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024` cap on parser response is a partial mitigation, but the runs list is unbounded — `_runs_from_tag` doesn't cap anchor count.
findings.location: Section: Decisions § Decision 5; Decision 6; _render_paragraph_with_runs design; orangetrack_source.py:62 (response cap), orangetrack_source.py:246 (_runs_from_tag, no run-count cap)
findings.impact: Denial of service on the cron processing path. Not catastrophic (single-tenant bot, retry-on-fail), but slows the 10:00 МСК tick and could miss publish windows. Also affects `hw_review preview N` (operator UX).
findings.recommendation:
1. Cap runs per block at e.g. 50; cap text length at e.g. 20 KB before invoking the helper. Drop overflow runs to plain text.

2. Sort runs by `len(text)` desc OR build a single regex alternation (compiled once) instead of N str.find calls — but regex alternation is its own complexity. Keeping str.find is fine if N is bounded.

3. Add `runs = runs[:50]` defensively at the top of `_render_paragraph_with_runs` and log a warning when truncated.

4. Add a regression test with a synthetic 100-run paragraph to verify it doesn't time out.
findings.cwe: CWE-1333 (Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity) — analog for substring; CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)

findings.title: Tech-spec doesn't specify logging when malformed href / urlparse exception / overlapping run is dropped.
findings.description: Decisions 4, 5, 6 all say "silently dropped" / "silently skipped" / "first-wrap-wins, others dropped". Silent drops on security-relevant decisions (especially urlparse exceptions) deny operators visibility when source-side patterns shift. If orangetrack changes their URL structure or starts publishing relative URLs, the bot stops rendering links and nobody knows. Conversely, if an unexpected run pattern appears (could indicate source compromise), it's invisible.
findings.location: Section: Decisions § Decision 4 ("silently dropped"), Decision 5 ("silently dropped"), Decision 6; _render_paragraph_with_runs design
findings.impact: Reduced incident-response capability: a sudden surge of dropped same-site runs (indicating source HTML restructure) or a surge of overlapping-run conflicts (indicating LLM translation drift) goes unnoticed until visual inspection. Limits ability to detect source-site compromise patterns.
findings.recommendation:
Add `logger.debug` (not warning — these are normal events) when:
  - urlparse raises (rate-limited; warning at >N per article)
  - same-site run dropped due to overlap (debug)
  - run.text not found in block.text (debug)

More importantly: at WARNING level when the drop rate exceeds ~50% of runs in a single article — that signals a structural change worth investigating. Operator already monitors journalctl; one log line is enough.

findings.title: Bullet `"• "` is hardcoded (good), but tech-spec doesn't specify what happens if LLM output already starts with a bullet character.
findings.description:
Decision 1 hardcodes `"• "` (U+2022 + space) as the bullet, prepended at publisher level — confirmed safe (not user-controlled, immune to LLM stripping). However, an unintended doubling can occur: if the LLM, despite being asked to translate just text, decides to prepend a bullet itself (some LLMs reflexively format lists in any output), the rendered Telegraph paragraph becomes `"• • Ferrari"`. Or worse: `"• 1. Ferrari"` if the LLM numbers items.

This is purely a presentation bug, not a security finding, but cosmetic doubling is the kind of issue that the tech-spec's "immune to LLM stripping" claim implicitly promises against. Worth a defensive check.
findings.location: Section: Decisions § Decision 1 (line 70); telegraph_publisher.py preview_nodes list_item branch
findings.impact: Cosmetic only — visible doubled bullets in published articles. Not exploitable.
findings.recommendation:
Before prepending `"• "`, strip a leading bullet from the LLM-translated text:

```python
LEADING_BULLETS_RE = re.compile(r"^[\u2022\u25E6\u2043\-\*]\s*")  # •, ◦, ⁃, -, *
text = LEADING_BULLETS_RE.sub("", block["text"]).lstrip()
```

Add a unit test: `block.text == "• Ferrari"` → rendered as `"• Ferrari"` not `"• • Ferrari"`.

findings.title: No XSS vector confirmed for `_render_paragraph_with_runs` node-tree output, but tech-spec doesn't document the trust boundary between RSS-fetched text and Telegraph rendering.
findings.description:
Reviewer-requested audit point: `_render_paragraph_with_runs(text, runs, source_url)` takes RSS-fetched text + href as input → emitted as Telegraph node tree.

XSS analysis: Telegraph's `createPage` API accepts a JSON-serialized `content` array. The publisher constructs Python dicts like `{"tag": "a", "attrs": {"href": ...}, "children": [text]}`, which `json.dumps` serializes. The text and href are passed as JSON strings — Telegraph's server-side renderer is responsible for HTML-encoding them when materializing the page. There is NO point where the publisher concatenates user-controlled text into an HTML string. Confirmed: no direct XSS vector via text content.

Residual risks:
  - Href-based XSS: `_safe_href` already drops `javascript:`, `data:`, `file:`. Telegraph's server also has its own scheme allowlist. Defense-in-depth holds. (See finding #3 for mailto: edge case.)
  - Malformed unicode (e.g., direction-override characters U+202E) in `run.text` could visually spoof URLs in some rendering clients. `_runs_from_tag` does `re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)` which doesn't strip BiDi controls. Worth flagging for paranoid completeness.
findings.location: Section: Decisions § Decision 6; orangetrack_source.py:284 (whitespace normalization, no BiDi stripping)
findings.impact: Low — Telegraph renders server-side and most clients are well-behaved. BiDi spoofing is theoretical and would target visual recognition, not code execution.
findings.recommendation:
1. Document in `_render_paragraph_with_runs` docstring: "Trust boundary: text is JSON-encoded by `json.dumps` in `publish_article`; Telegraph server HTML-encodes when rendering. Therefore no string-interpolation XSS surface here."

2. Optional: strip Unicode bidirectional/format characters (`unicodedata.category(c) in ('Cf',)`) from `run.text` before substring search — paranoid hardening against visual spoofing.

3. Add a test asserting that text containing `<script>alert(1)</script>` survives the helper as plain text (not stripped, not interpreted) — confirms node-tree non-interpretation contract.
